say.text: Quick mixed check: six questions with hints, then six cold ones with no hints.
A kitchen gas cylinder blew up. This patient reached you 20 minutes ago with 30% flame burns to the face, singed eyebrows and a rough voice. The fluid chart is open on the desk.
Which plan puts the steps in the right order?

choices.label: Work out the fluid sum now, then review the airway and breathing
Secure the airway early, then breathing and circulation, then the fluid sum
Watch the airway and intubate only once stridor or desaturation begins
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which step can be lost within the hour, and which one can wait for the chart.
That choice is not right. The fluid chart feels like the urgent burn task, so the numbers seem to belong first.
The fluid sum is a secondary-survey job. The primary survey, with the airway, comes before burn size and fluid.

sure_note.text: You were sure the numbers come first. Check the primary survey before you trust that instinct.

say.text: That choice is not right. A patient who talks well looks safe, so waiting for stridor seems reasonable.
Oedema builds over hours after burns. Hoarseness with soot, or deep facial burns, is a reason to act before it closes the airway.

sure_note.text: You were sure waiting was safe. The oedema grows after the injury, not only once stridor starts.

say.text: Hoarseness, soot and facial burns mean the airway can close as oedema builds over hours. Secure it early, while the tube still goes in.
Breathing and circulation come next in the primary survey. Burn size and the Parkland sum come after that.
Yes. Secure the airway early, while the tube still goes in: oedema builds over hours, and hoarseness with soot is a sign.
Breathing and circulation come next in the primary survey, and the fluid sum comes after.
The ward has the chest film and the arterial gas back. Both look acceptable.
The question is whether smoke has damaged the airway itself. What still needs doing?

choices.label: Repeat the chest X-ray in six hours and compare the films
Repeat the arterial blood gas at six hours and compare results
Fibreoptic bronchoscopy to look at the airway below the cords
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test looks at the airway itself, rather than one that measures gas or shadows.
That choice is not right. A normal film feels reassuring, so repeating it looks like the next logical check.
A chest X-ray is often normal early in inhalation injury, so it cannot rule the injury out.

sure_note.text: You were sure a repeat film would settle it. A normal film early does not rule out airway injury.

say.text: That choice is not right. Gas results feel like hard evidence, so repeating one looks like more proof.
Arterial gas tells you about gas exchange and carboxyhaemoglobin. It does not show soot or oedema in the airway.

sure_note.text: You were sure the gas would decide it. The gas measures oxygen and carbon monoxide, not the airway lining.

say.text: Fibreoptic bronchoscopy looks directly at the airway and shows soot, oedema and erythema below the cords.
A chest X-ray is often normal early, and arterial gas does not look at the airway.
Yes. Bronchoscopy confirms inhalation injury by showing soot, oedema and erythema below the cords.
A fire victim is on a monitor. Which measurement tells you the carboxyhaemoglobin level?

choices.label: Co-oximetry on an arterial blood sample, which reads carboxyhaemoglobin directly
Finger pulse oximetry, trended hourly on the bedside monitor
A normal saturation reading, rechecked after giving oxygen
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which measurement reads the haemoglobin that carries carbon monoxide, rather than what a probe reads through the skin.
That choice is not right. A steady trace feels thorough, and a number that holds looks like reassurance.
A finger probe reads light at two wavelengths and cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, however often it is trended.

sure_note.text: You were sure the trend would tell you something. Trending a blind reading still gives a blind reading.

say.text: That choice is not right. A saturation of 99% feels like proof that oxygen is being carried well.
The saturation number is blind to carboxyhaemoglobin, so rechecking it cannot settle the question.

sure_note.text: You were sure the normal number meant safe. The reading itself cannot show carbon monoxide.

say.text: Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, because it cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin.
Co-oximetry on arterial blood measures carboxyhaemoglobin directly. A headache after a closed-space fire is the cue to send it.
Yes. Co-oximetry measures carboxyhaemoglobin directly in arterial blood, which the finger probe cannot do.
An adult has a burn across the whole of one arm. Using the adult rule of nines, what does one arm count for?

choices.label: 18% of TBSA for one upper limb, as the adult chart gives
9% of TBSA for one upper limb, as the adult chart gives
4.5% of TBSA for one upper limb, as the adult chart gives
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Recall which regions carry the 18s. An upper limb is not one of them.
That choice is not right. Limbs look alike on the chart, so the leg figure is easy to carry over to an arm.
The 18s belong to each leg and to each side of the trunk. Check which figure the upper limb takes.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the leg figure. Arms and legs are both limbs, but they sit in different rows of the chart.

say.text: That choice is not right. Halving a figure feels like the way to size a single limb.
The palm method is a separate estimate for small patches. The adult chart gives one upper limb a whole-number share.

sure_note.text: You were sure of halving the limb. The rule of nines does not halve the limb; the palm method is a different tool.

say.text: On the adult rule of nines, each upper limb is 9%, the head is 9%, each leg is 18%, each side of the trunk is 18%, and the perineum is 1%.
Yes. On the adult rule of nines each upper limb is 9%, while each leg and each side of the trunk is 18%.
An 80 kg adult has 30% TBSA scalds. The infusion starts at the time of the burn, and the Parkland 4 mL key is used.
What hourly rate covers the first 8 hours?

choices.label: 1,200 mL/h, the whole 24-hour volume in 8 hours
200 mL/h, half the 24-hour volume spread over 24 hours
600 mL/h, half the 24-hour volume over 8 hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Find the first-half volume before you divide, and ask which window that half covers.
That choice is not right. The biggest number feels like the response a severe burn deserves.
The first window carries a share of the day's volume, not all of it. Check what fraction goes in 8 hours.

sure_note.text: You were sure the whole volume belongs in the first window. Check the Parkland fraction for the first 8 hours.

say.text: That choice is not right. Spreading half over the whole day feels gentler for a burned patient.
The first half runs over 8 hours from the time of burn, so the divisor has to match that window.

sure_note.text: You were sure a slow start was safer. The window is set by the time of burn, not by the day.

say.text: Parkland: 4 mL times kg times %TBSA gives 9,600 mL over 24 hours. Half, 4,800 mL, goes over the first 8 hours from the burn.
That is 600 mL/h. The other 4,800 mL runs over the next 16 hours.
Yes. Four times 80 times 30 gives 9,600 mL; half is 4,800 mL, and over 8 hours that is 600 mL/h.
A 60 kg adult is on the formula rate after a 40% burn. Four hours in, urine on the catheter has run at 110 mL/h for the last hour. Pulse and blood pressure are steady.
What do you do with the rate?

choices.label: Reduce the rate, then recheck urine and vitals at the next review
Increase the rate, since good output means the kidneys want more fluid
Keep the formula rate, since the calculated figure is the order
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what high output tells you about perfusion, and whether the formula was meant as a fixed order.
That choice is not right. Good output feels like a sign the kidneys can take more, so more fluid looks logical.
High output means perfusion is adequate, and more fluid risks pulmonary oedema and compartment syndromes.

sure_note.text: You were sure output meant the kidneys wanted more. High output points the other way.

say.text: That choice is not right. A calculated figure feels like the prescription, so changing it looks like an error.
The formula is a starting estimate that is titrated hourly, so the urine reading is information you act on.

sure_note.text: You were sure the calculated rate was the order. The formula starts the plan, and urine steers it.

say.text: Urine output is a perfusion signal. Low output means under-resuscitation and more fluid; high output means the rate can come down.
Over-resuscitation causes pulmonary oedema and compartment syndromes, so each hour's reading guides the rate.
Yes. High hourly output means the rate can come down, with urine and vitals rechecked at the next review.
A 12 kg child has 15% scalds. What hourly urine output do you aim for?

choices.label: 6 mL/h, the adult figure of 0.5 mL/kg/h
12 mL/h, about 1 mL/kg/h for a child
30 to 50 mL/h, the usual adult range

say.text: That choice is not right. Scaling the adult figure down by weight feels like a child adjustment.
The child target is 1 mL/kg/h, so a 12 kg child aims for about 12 mL/h.

sure_note.text: You were sure you had scaled the adult figure. A child's target is per kilogram at 1 mL/kg/h.

say.text: That choice is not right. The adult range is the number most people remember, so it becomes the default.
The child target is 1 mL/kg/h, about 12 mL/h here. The adult range is for adults.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the familiar range. Age changes the target, not only the burn size.

say.text: Yes. The child target is 1 mL/kg/h, so a 12 kg child aims for about 12 mL/h.
A flame burn on the forearm is dry and white, and the centre feels nothing. The edge, where skin is intact, hurts.
What depth is the centre?

choices.label: Full thickness, with a painless dry centre and painful edges
Deep partial thickness, since the centre hurts less than the edge
Superficial partial thickness, since the edge is the painful part

say.text: That choice is not right. Less pain feels like a shallower burn than the skin around it.
The centre is full thickness: dry, leathery and painless, and it does not blanch. Pain at the edge comes from intact skin.

sure_note.text: You were sure the paler centre was deep partial. Less pain is not the same as a depth marker.

say.text: That choice is not right. Pain at the edge feels like the depth marker, so the burn looks superficial.
Pain at the edge comes from intact skin around the burn. A painless, dry, leathery centre is full thickness.

sure_note.text: You were sure the painful edge meant a shallow burn. The edge and the centre are different tissue.

say.text: Yes. A painless, dry, leathery centre that does not blanch is full thickness; pain at the margin is intact skin.
An adult has burns to the head and neck, both arms, and the front of the trunk. Using the adult rule of nines, what is the total TBSA?

choices.label: About 63% of TBSA, counting each arm at 18%
About 54% of TBSA, with the head counted at 18%
About 45% of TBSA, counting head, arms and front trunk

say.text: That choice is not right. Each arm feels like a large limb, so counting it double looks like a serious burn.
Each upper limb is 9% on the adult chart, so both arms make 18%, and the total is 45%.

sure_note.text: You were sure each arm was 18%. Upper limbs share the 9 figure on the adult chart.

say.text: That choice is not right. A head that looks large gets the trunk figure in memory.
The head is 9% on the adult chart, so the total is 45%, not 54%.

sure_note.text: You were sure the head was 18%. The head shares the 9 figure with the upper limbs.

say.text: Yes. Head 9, both arms 18 together, and the front trunk 18 make 45% of TBSA.
A 60 kg adult has 30% burns. The first 8 hours have run as planned, and the second half of the 24-hour volume is next.
Over the next 16 hours, what hourly rate does the second half need?

choices.label: 450 mL/h, the first-window rate carried on unchanged
225 mL/h, the second half spread over the next 16 hours
900 mL/h, the whole 24-hour volume in the next 8 hours

say.text: That choice is not right. Keeping the early pace feels consistent, so the same rate looks sensible.
The first window has already used half the day's volume. The second half, 3,600 mL, runs over 16 hours: 225 mL/h.

sure_note.text: You were sure the early rate should carry on. The rate is set by what is left and the window left.

say.text: That choice is not right. Giving the whole day's volume quickly feels like catching up on a deficit.
The whole-day volume is not still due. The second half, 3,600 mL, runs over 16 hours, giving 225 mL/h.

sure_note.text: You were sure the whole day should go in fast. The first half has already been given over its window.

say.text: Yes. Half of 7,200 mL is 3,600 mL; spread over 16 hours, that is 225 mL/h.
Mafenide cream is on the chart for a deep, crusted burn that needs eschar penetration.
Which systemic effect do you monitor for?

choices.label: Leucopenia, a fall in white cells seen in the blood count
Hyponatraemia with a black stain, seen on the dressing
Metabolic acidosis, from carbonic anhydrase inhibition in the blood

say.text: That choice is not right. Blood-count side effects are the best-known topical effect, so the marrow effect is an easy swap.
Leucopenia belongs to silver sulfadiazine. Mafenide's systemic effect is metabolic acidosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure about the blood count. That effect is the silver sulfadiazine one, not the mafenide one.

say.text: That choice is not right. A sodium change and a stain are both memorable silver effects, so the pair is easy to mix up.
Hyponatraemia and black staining go with silver nitrate. Mafenide causes metabolic acidosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure about the stain. Silver nitrate carries that pair; mafenide does not.

say.text: Yes. Mafenide penetrates eschar and can cause metabolic acidosis, so check the acid-base picture.
A patient with soot and a hoarse voice is talking in full sentences. Your review is two hours away.
What is the right plan for the airway?

choices.label: Recheck the voice at the two-hour review and act then
Secure the airway now, while the tube still passes easily
Start the fluid sum now, then check the airway at review

say.text: That choice is not right. A patient who speaks well looks safe, so waiting for the review seems sensible.
Oedema builds over hours after burns and soot, so the airway can close before the review. Secure it now.

sure_note.text: You were sure the voice meant safe. Oedema is the process to watch, and it moves faster than a review.

say.text: That choice is not right. The fluid sum is ready and feels like the next job on the list.
The airway can close within hours; the fluid sum can wait minutes. The airway is the first step in the primary survey.

sure_note.text: You were sure the chart came first. The primary survey puts the airway before the numbers.

say.text: Yes. Early intubation while the tube still passes: oedema builds over hours, and hoarseness with soot is a sign.
Quick recap. Airway first, then breathing and circulation. Bronchoscopy confirms inhalation injury; co-oximetry measures carbon monoxide.
Parkland halves the 24-hour volume over the right window, and hourly urine output steers the rate.

cards.q: In a burn with soot and hoarseness, what comes first?
cards.a: Secure the airway early, while the tube still passes; oedema builds over hours. Breathing and circulation follow, and the fluid sum comes after.

cards.q: Which test confirms inhalation injury, and why can pulse oximetry mislead?
cards.a: Fibreoptic bronchoscopy confirms it. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning because it cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin.

cards.q: Full thickness versus deep partial thickness?
cards.a: Full thickness is painless, dry, leathery and does not blanch. Deep partial is less painful, mottled, with sluggish refill.

cards.q: Adult rule of nines: one upper limb, each leg, the perineum?
cards.a: Each upper limb 9%; each leg 18%; perineum 1%.

cards.q: Parkland: what is the first half, and over what window?
cards.a: Half of 4 mL times kg times %TBSA, counted from the time of burn and given over the first 8 hours.

cards.q: Hourly urine targets for an adult, a child and electrical injury?
cards.a: Adult 0.5 mL/kg/h (30 to 50 mL/h); child 1 mL/kg/h; electrical about 1 to 1.5 mL/kg/h. Titrate hourly.

cards.q: Which side effect goes with mafenide?
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis, from carbonic anhydrase inhibition. Silver sulfadiazine causes leucopenia; silver nitrate causes hyponatraemia and black staining.
